consensus: P5 is strictly better than P0 and the compiled prompt on content correctness: it is the only transport that carries both silently dropped items (constraint and work item) on this fixture, while P0 and the compiled prompt carry neither.

P5's context cost is materially higher than the compiled prompt — roughly 3-4x in rendered words/bytes (174-184 words / 2,435-2,519 bytes vs 60-580 bytes), echoing or exceeding the 3.26x multiple from P1b.

Downstream/receiver benefit remains completely unproven — the PR itself states this, and no live model comparison exists, so 'carries the drop' is a property of the artifact, not of receiver behavior.

The history tier being ranked below bookkeeping sections and omitted first under budget pressure is problematic — described variously as a 'priority defect,' 'specification gap bordering on defect,' or 'specification gap' — because it undermines P5's core stated purpose of recovering drops, and v2 should recommend reprioritizing drops above bookkeeping and/or fitting history item-by-item with an explicit omission marker.

The budget-unit vs rendered-size mismatch (100-word budget yields 174 rendered words/2,435 bytes) should be called 'both' a correctness defect (against the receiver-fit contract) and a design limitation/accepted simplification (word-count as a documented proxy), with identifiers as the largest unbudgeted contributor.

The next experiment should be a live, preregistered, paired/multi-arm receiver comparison (P5 vs compiled prompt, possibly plus compiled-prompt+raw-history) measuring actual drop recovery/behavior, not just artifact content — and P5 is falsified if a cheaper arm (compiled prompt plus existing records) matches P5's recovery rate, directly invoking the kill criterion.

v2 should foreground that the fixture's apparent win for P5 is incomplete/overstated without live behavioral evidence, and should surface the facts that currently threaten the hypothesis (growth costs, defects, baseline asymmetry) rather than leading with the success table.
disagreements: Panelists differ on which single measurement is 'most decision-relevant' for the overhead-vs-benefit kill criterion: gpt-6-sol-high points to the P1b 3.26x-words-tie result; fable points to the P5 small-receiver row (99/100 budget, 174 words/2,435 bytes vs 580-byte compiled prompt); opus points instead to the unbounded growth terms (158ms vs 67ms verification slowdown, 347KB boundary block at 1,600 revisions) as more decisive than any fixed ratio.

On Q6 (what v2 should say differently), the panelists pick different single most-important corrections: gpt-6-sol-high emphasizes distinguishing 'recovering omitted facts' from 'improving receiver behavior'; fable emphasizes leading with scaling/defect facts (unbounded growth, provenance defects) instead of the fixture table; opus uniquely argues the measured advantage is partly a 'baseline artifact' because the compiled prompt was never given the dropped items to begin with, making the comparison unfair to the baseline.

Severity framing on the history-tier ranking (Q3) varies: gpt-6-sol-high calls it a clear 'priority defect,' fable splits it as 'specification gap bordering on defect,' and opus leans toward 'specification gap that presents as a defect' — subtly different emphases on whether this is primarily an implementation bug or a missing spec decision.

On Q4, opus uniquely frames the recommended fix as renaming the concept entirely (e.g., to `content_word_budget`) and publishing/testing a rendering multiplier, which neither of the other two panelists proposes as the specific remedy.
partial_coverage: Only fable and opus explicitly compute/cite the specific ms figures (67→158ms, 68ms/88ms) and the 347KB boundary block figure as central evidence; gpt-6-sol-high does not engage with the scaling/performance data at all in its answer.

Only fable and opus discuss the three provenance defects and the 24-mutation/17-caught pass as materially undermining the 'carries the drop' claim (i.e., that drops might be carried incorrectly); gpt-6-sol-high mentions the defects only briefly in Q1 and does not connect them to the later discussion of correctness or the falsification experiment.

Only opus explicitly raises the 'baseline artifact' critique — that the compiled prompt was never given the dropped items, making the P5-vs-compiled-prompt comparison structurally unfair — none of the other panelists raise this framing.

Only fable explicitly proposes compressing/restructuring the three bookkeeping sections as part of the v2 recommendation (beyond just reranking), and only fable explicitly ties the P1b 3.26x figure into the Q1 cost analysis as 'the same multiple... unchanged from the lane that already tied.'

Only gpt-6-sol-high keeps its answer entirely abstract/general without citing many of the specific numeric details (ms timings, KB figures, mutation pass results) that fable and opus both foreground, making its answer comparatively thinner on quantitative grounding despite reaching similar qualitative verdicts.
unique_insights: Opus's 'baseline artifact' critique: the comparison between P5 and the compiled prompt may be invalid on its face because the compiled prompt was never given the dropped items as input, so P5 'winning' at carrying drops the other transport was never asked to carry is not necessarily evidence of superiority — a distinct epistemological point none of the others raise.

Opus's observation that 27 of the 55-word minimum (49% of the floor) is pure TORC self-description, framed as a 'runner-up' decision-relevant measurement — quantifying how much of the minimum viable budget is overhead rather than content.

Fable's specific quantification that the budget accounting understates true cost by ~1.7x (100 budgeted → 174 read) plus ~40 provider tokens of hex per unaccounted section, giving a precise multiplier for the mismatch.
Opus's proposal to rename the budget parameter itself (to something like `content_word_budget`) as the concrete fix for the Q4 correctness defect, rather than just changing what's measured.

Gpt-6-sol-high's framing of the central Q1 distinction as 'recovering omitted facts' vs 'improving receiver behavior' as the single most important conceptual clarification for v2 — a crisp dichotomy not phrased this way by the others.
blind_spots: None of the panelists address what happens if the receiving substrate's descriptor itself is wrong, stale, or adversarially misreported (e.g., carry_limit misconfigured) — the whole receiver-fit mechanism depends on trusting a self-reported descriptor with no verification discussed.

None discuss the compounding risk of the provenance defects interacting with the history-tier carrying mechanism at scale — e.g., whether a stale 'completed' disposition could itself get silently dropped and then re-surface incorrectly in a future carry, creating a defect that compounds across many handoffs rather than being a one-time fixable bug.

No panelist proposes a concrete bound or cap for the unbounded boundary-block growth (347KB at 1,600 revisions) — all flag it as a problem but none sketch what a bounded/paginated design should look like (e.g., pagination scheme, staleness window, summarization strategy) beyond opus's passing mention of 'paged.'

None examine the asymmetry in the fixture itself — all four transport rows use the same head revision, but none question whether this single fixture is representative enough to generalize any of these verdicts, or what range of fixtures (lineage lengths, drop counts, receiver types) would be needed before trusting the deterministic measurements as generalizable.

None discuss the organizational/process cost of the 'boundary block' asking receivers about unaccounted drops and self-model restatement — i.e., the human/agent attention cost of answering these non-blocking prompts repeatedly, which is a form of operational burden distinct from compute/token overhead and arguably relevant to the kill criterion's 'operational burden' language.

None address versioning/compatibility risk: what happens when p5-1's receiver-fit logic itself changes between TORC versions and must reconcile with lineage history compiled under a prior logic version — a continuity-of-the-continuity-mechanism problem.
